consumer_seed: The Ofcom social-tariff guide was published on 6 March 2024.
The Ofcom social-tariff guide was last updated on 22 June 2026.
Social tariffs are cheaper broadband and phone packages for people claiming Universal Credit, Pension Credit and some other benefits.
Social tariffs are delivered in the same way as normal packages but at a lower price.
Social tariffs are available to people receiving a variety of benefits.
If someone in a household claims Universal Credit, the household may switch to an available social tariff.
Ofcom listed current social-tariff prices ranging from £10 to £24.
Most listed social tariffs offered superfast broadband above 30 Mbit/s.
Any setup costs for a social tariff should be small and disclosed before sign-up.
Where the current provider offers a social tariff, the customer can switch to it at any time free of charge.
The price of a social tariff should not rise during the contract.
A social-tariff customer should not pay a fee to leave before the contract ends.
BT and KCOM provide cheaper voice-only landline tariffs to eligible households.
Major providers include people receiving Pension Credit in social-tariff eligibility.
Major providers include people receiving Employment and Support Allowance in social-tariff eligibility.
Major providers include people receiving Jobseeker's Allowance in social-tariff eligibility.
Major providers include people receiving Income Support in social-tariff eligibility.
Some providers include Personal Independence Payment among qualifying benefits.
Some providers include Attendance Allowance among qualifying benefits.
The person receiving the qualifying benefit must be the main person on the contract.
Most social tariffs can be applied for online or by calling the provider.
A customer whose provider has no social tariff can switch to a provider that does.
A provider may allow a customer to leave an existing contract without a penalty when moving to a social tariff elsewhere.
Providers might not cover every premises in the regions listed in Ofcom's social-tariff table.
Customers struggling to pay a mobile or broadband bill should contact their provider as soon as possible.
The Ofcom bill-difficulty guide was published on 13 March 2013.
The Ofcom bill-difficulty guide was last updated on 8 April 2026.
A customer having difficulty paying a bill should not ignore it.
A customer should contact the phone provider as soon as possible about payment difficulty.
A customer can ask the provider about moving to a cheaper package.
A customer can ask about paying the debt over time.
A customer can ask about reducing monthly payments to an affordable rate.
A customer can ask whether part of the debt can be waived if the remainder is paid within a specified time.
A customer can ask to change the payment date or switch to direct debit.
A customer can ask about selling old mobile handsets for recycling.
A customer can ask the provider for details of debt-advice agencies.
A provider is not obliged to offer the listed payment-support options.
Free advice on debt and managing money is available.
Some providers charge reconnection fees in addition to the debt owed.
A disconnected customer may be treated as a new customer and face credit checks or deposits.
Telecoms firms usually contact the customer when a bill is unpaid.
An unpaid account may have outgoing calls restricted to emergency calls and calls to the provider.
Inbound calls may remain unaffected while outgoing calls are restricted.
Some providers make extra efforts to contact vulnerable customers before restriction or disconnection.
A customer whose complaint remains unresolved for more than six weeks can speak to an ADR provider.
The Ofcom broadband-speeds consumer guide was published on 21 November 2022.
The Broadband Speeds Code of Practice requires clear speed information when buying broadband.
A customer receiving lower-than-promised speeds should contact the provider.
If a network speed problem cannot be fixed within 30 days, a signed-up provider must allow the customer to leave without an early exit fee.
BT is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
EE is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
NOW Broadband is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Plusnet is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Sky is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
TalkTalk is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Utility Warehouse is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Virgin Media is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Zen Internet is listed under the broadband-speed protections.
Signed-up providers commit to giving estimated speed ranges in writing at the start of a contract.
Signed-up providers commit to robust processes for handling speed-related problems swiftly and effectively.
The Ofcom contracts guide was published on 24 July 2023.
The Ofcom contracts guide was last updated on 1 May 2026.
Providers must ensure contract terms are fair and transparent.
Residential and qualifying small-business customers should receive a one-page contract summary before consent.
The contract summary may be three pages for bundled services.
The contract summary should include key information about charges.
The contract summary should include the contract length.
The contract summary should include the process for cancelling.
Before the customer is bound, the provider must give more detailed contract information in writing.
Customers with disabilities can request contract information in a reasonably acceptable format such as large print or Braille.
Ofcom recommends not signing until the customer fully understands the contract terms.
Customers should consider whether additional charges apply under a proposed contract.
Additional charges may include costs for leaving the service early.
Additional charges may include costs for paper billing.
Additional charges may include roaming costs.
Additional charges may include costs for failing to provide sufficient cancellation or switching notice.
